lesson.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes - Python Pandas Tutorial

sources.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes - Python Pandas Tutorial

steps.title: Set up project and install pandas
steps.instructions: Clone https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial or place orders.csv into an empty project folder, then open a terminal there. Install pandas with pip install pandas (or uv init . then uv add pandas).

targets.caption: Install pandas using pip or uv in the project terminal

explanations.topic: Using pip vs uv virtual environments

hints: Which package manager are you using for Python in this project?
Run pip install pandas (or pip3 install pandas on macOS/Linux) in the integrated terminal.
If you prefer uv, run uv init . followed by uv add pandas.
common_mistakes: Using pip instead of pip3 on macOS or Linux systems.
Forgetting to download orders.csv into the working directory before running code.

steps.title: Load and print CSV in Python
steps.instructions: Create main.py, import pandas as pd, load orders.csv into df with pd.read_csv and print(df). Run it from the terminal (python main.py or uv run main.py).

targets.caption: Load orders.csv into a DataFrame named df
Verify the DataFrame dimensions printed in terminal

explanations.topic: Why pandas fits CSV and tabular data

hints: How do you alias pandas when importing it?
Use pd.read_csv("orders.csv") and assign the result to df.
Add print(df) and execute the file with python main.py or uv run main.py.
common_mistakes: Running Python from a parent folder where orders.csv is missing, causing FileNotFoundError.
Omitting quotes around the filename inside pd.read_csv().
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
print(df)`

steps.title: Create Jupyter notebook and load CSV
steps.instructions: Run Create: New Jupyter Notebook from the command palette, save it as notebook.ipynb and select your Python kernel. Load orders.csv with pd.read_csv in the first cell and run print(df) in a second cell.

targets.caption: Load orders.csv in the first notebook cell and select a Python kernel

explanations.topic: Why Jupyter notebooks help with data tasks
Installing the Python extension for notebooks

hints: How do you create a .ipynb file in VS Code or Cursor?
Press Ctrl+Shift+P (or Cmd+Shift+P) and run Create: New Jupyter Notebook, then save as notebook.ipynb.
Run import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv") in cell 1 before running print(df) in cell 2.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to select a Python kernel before executing a notebook cell.
Running the second cell (print(df)) before executing the first cell that defines df.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
print(df)`

steps.title: Explore DataFrame summary and structure
steps.instructions: In new notebook cells, call df.head(), df.tail(), df.info() and df.describe(), and run each cell with Shift+Enter. Also evaluate df.columns and df.index to see column names and the row range.

targets.caption: Inspect column data types and non-null counts

explanations.topic: Why string columns appear as object dtype

hints: Which DataFrame methods preview rows and summarize column types?
Call df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), and df.describe() in cells.
Access .columns and .index without parentheses since they are attributes.
common_mistakes: Calling df.columns() or df.index() with parentheses, which raises TypeError.
Omitting parentheses on df.info or df.describe, which prints the method object instead of running it.
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index`

steps.title: Index DataFrame by column and row
steps.instructions: Select a single column with df["Country"] and multiple columns with df[["Country", "Product"]]. Use df.iloc[10] and df.iloc[10]["Shipped"] to retrieve a row and a cell by integer position.

targets.caption: Select row 10 by integer index using iloc

explanations.topic: Series vs DataFrame returned when indexing columns
How iloc locates rows by integer index

hints: How many pairs of brackets are needed to select multiple columns?
Pass a list of column names inside df[...], such as df[["Country", "Product"]].
Use df.iloc[10] for row 10, then chain ["Shipped"] to read a single cell.
common_mistakes: Writing df["Country", "Product"] with single brackets instead of double brackets, causing a KeyError.
Using parentheses df.iloc(10) instead of square brackets df.iloc[10].

steps.title: Filter rows with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, filter rows with boolean masks such as df[df["Category"] == "Electronics"], combining conditions with & and |. Practice .str.startswith(), .isin() and ~ to negate a filter, running each cell with Shift+Enter.

targets.caption: Filter rows matching or excluding a list of values with isin()

explanations.topic: Negating a filter condition with tilde (~)`

hints: Which operators combine boolean Series in pandas?
Wrap each condition in parentheses and join with & (and) or | (or).
Use .str.startswith("A") for prefix matches and ~df[...].isin([...]) to negate membership.
common_mistakes: Using Python keywords and/or instead of &/| in pandas filters, causing a ValueError.
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when using & or |.

steps.title: Update rows and transform columns
steps.instructions: Update matching rows with df.loc[mask, "Country"] = "United States", then uppercase the Country column by assigning df["Country"].str.upper() back to it. Run the cells and display df to see the changes.

targets.caption: Uppercase the Country column with str.upper()

explanations.topic: Using df.loc to locate rows by label or condition

hints: Which indexer accepts both a row condition and a target column name?
Use df.loc[condition, "ColumnName"] = new_value to update cells.
Reassign df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper() so the uppercase change persists.
common_mistakes: Chaining df[condition]["Product"] = ... instead of df.loc[condition, "Product"] = ..., triggering SettingWithCopyWarning.
Calling df["Country"].str.upper() without assigning it back to df["Country"].
steps.code:
df.loc[df["CustomerName"] == "Anna Ivanova", "Product"] = "Tim"
df.loc[df["Country"] == "USA", "Country"] = "United States"
df["Country"] = df["Country"].str.upper()`

steps.title: Delete a row using drop
steps.instructions: Delete a row by assigning df = df.drop(<index>), e.g. df.drop(39). Run df.tail() in the next cell to confirm the row was removed.

targets.caption: Drop a row and assign the result back to df

hints: Does df.drop(39) modify df in place by default?
Reassign the returned DataFrame: df = df.drop(39).
Call df.tail() in the next cell to check the bottom rows.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning df or setting inplace=True, leaving df unchanged.

steps.title: Clean missing values and rename columns
steps.instructions: Reload df, then try df.dropna() and df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True). Rename a column with df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True), display df and run the cell (Shift+Enter).

targets.caption: Rename columns in place using a mapping dictionary
Fill missing values in a column

explanations.topic: Cleaning null entries with dropna and fillna
How inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame

hints: How do you specify old and new column names in df.rename()?
Pass columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"} and inplace=True to df.rename(...).
Use df.dropna() to drop nulls or df.fillna(...) to replace missing values.
common_mistakes: Omitting inplace=True without reassigning df = df.rename(...), leaving the old column name.
Passing a list instead of a dictionary to the columns parameter in df.rename().
steps.code:
df.dropna()
df.fillna({"OrderID": 0}, inplace=True)
df.rename(columns={"OrderID": "Order ID"}, inplace=True)`

steps.title: Group, sort, and export DataFrame
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, summarize with df["Country"].value_counts() and df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum(), then sort with df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False). Export the result with df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False).

targets.caption: Group rows and sum a column per group
Sort rows by a column, descending
Save the DataFrame to a CSV without row indices

explanations.topic: Aggregating column totals with groupby() and sum()

hints: Which method groups rows by a column before calling .sum()?
Use df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum() and df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False).
Pass index=False to df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False) so row numbers are omitted.
common_mistakes: Forgetting index=False in df.to_csv(), which writes an extra unnamed index column.
Leaving ascending=True when trying to sort prices from highest to lowest.
steps.code:
df["Country"].value_counts()
df.groupby("Country")["Price"].sum()
df.sort_values("Price", ascending=False)
df.to_csv("new_file.csv", index=False)`
